document.title: Limited Comments of Buckeye Power, Inc. on PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s proposal filed on 08/13/2026
document.group: PJM Large Load definition, Registry and Interim Resource Adequacy Service

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA  
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
 
LIMITED COMMENTS OF BUCKEYE POWER, INC. 
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s 
(“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Buckeye Power, Inc. (“Buckeye”)2 
respectfully submits these limited comments on PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) 
proposed revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the Reliability 
Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish the Interim 
Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”).3 In order to eliminate a potential unjust and 
unreasonable result, Buckeye seeks clarification as to how PJM intends to measure the 
MW quantity it directs Electric Distributors to reduce in an IRAS Action.  
Specifically, Buckeye seeks to avoid the possibility of PJM directing an Electric 
Distributor to drop a specified amount of MW based on registered peak loads of New 
Large Loads that exceeds the amount of actual New Large Load demand in real time, 
which would require the Electric Distributor to drop existing customer load. Such an 
outcome would be contrary to PJM’s intent to address the reliability challenges caused by 
New Large Loads unsupported by new capacity, and it would not be just and reasonable. 
PJM should therefore identify what in its proposed Tariff language or forthcoming PJM 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.211. 
2 Buckeye timely intervened in this proceeding. See (doc-less) Motion to Intervene of Buckeye Power, Inc. 
(Aug. 20, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260820-5106.  
3 PJM, Proposal to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry to Address

- 2 - 
 
Manuals details will prevent this problem, and the Commission should require PJM to 
clarify this issue if it does not do so on its own. To the extent further revisions to PJM’s 
proposed Tariff language are needed to address this issue, PJM should either make such 
revisions or the Commission should direct it to do so. 
COMMENTS 
I. 
Introduction 
PJM is proposing IRAS as an operational tool to address the reality that New 
Large Loads are developing more quickly than generation and transmission can be built, 
making it difficult for PJM to maintain a reliable electric grid while allowing these New 
Large Loads to interconnect at their desired pace.4 The IRAS framework is intended to 
allow PJM to identify the amount in MW of New Large Loads that exceeds capacity and 
order load reduction based on that amount during potential grid emergencies. This 
approach is intended to protect existing customers, including residential customers, from 
bearing the reliability impacts caused by New Large Loads, particularly to the extent 
New Large Loads are not supported by Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) or a 
share of Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”).  
As detailed in the proposed Tariff language, PJM may initiate an IRAS Action, 
“prior to calling on Pre-Emergency Load Management Reductions Actions after 
determining that available economic real-time supply may not be sufficient to maintain 
reserves to meet applicable Reserve Requirements and/or Interconnection Reliability 
 
4 Id., Attach. C, Affidavit of Christopher Pilong on Behalf of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., P 19 (“Pilong 
Aff.”).

- 3 - 
 
Operating Limits within prescribed limits and prevent cascading outages.”5 PJM has 
added the IRAS Action early in the emergency action process, prior to calling on 
Demand Response and Deploying All Resources.6 The very last action PJM proposes to 
take is a Manual Load Dump Action, which would require dropping existing loads and 
residential loads that have not opted for demand response. PJM’s goal of “prevent[ing] 
Manual Load Dump”7 properly recognizes that keeping existing customers, particularly 
residential loads, online is the primary goal in the event of a grid emergency. 
As PJM notes, “the IRAS framework is not motivated by any desire to single out 
New Large Loads for reduction because of their size or vintage, but rather for the valid 
and legitimate reason that New Large Loads have led to periods of insufficient resource 
adequacy and should, justifiably, play a significant role in the remedy.”8 In order to 
avoid perceived jurisdictional limitations, PJM states that when conducting an IRAS 
Action, it will issue MW load reduction to “Electric Distributors to implement reductions 
in load up to, and capped at, the pre-Delivery Year IRAS obligations they were 
assigned.”9 PJM states that it will be up to the Electric Distributors, not PJM, to direct 
which individual loads will drop in response to the directive:10 
 
5 Id., Attach. A, Revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff and Resource Adequacy 
Agreement (Marked/Redline Format) (“Redlined Tariff”), Attach. DD-4 § I(b). 
6 Id., Transmittal Letter at 79 (“Transmittal Letter”) (“Thus, it is appropriate for PJM to direct Electric 
Distributors to reduce those New Large Loads that have failed to cover their capacity obligations before 
relying on Demand Resources, through Pre-Emergency Load Management Reductions Actions, to maintain 
reliability.”). 
7 Transmittal Letter at 81. 
8 Id. at 100 (emphasis added).  
9 Pilong Aff. P 42.  
10 Id. (footnote omitted). See also Transmittal Letter at 87 (“Thus, under the IRAS framework, the specific 
retail customers that must reduce load consumption or switch to backup resources will be determined by 
the Electric Distributor and relevant LSEs in the zone/area, in coordination with the appropriate state and/or 
RERRA. Indeed, while PJM has proposed definitions of Large Load, New Large Load, and Eligible New 
Large Load that may be subject to IRAS, PJM simultaneously recognizes that states may each define ‘large

- 4 - 
 
Importantly, PJM will not direct specific New Large Loads to 
reduce load, even though Electric Distributors—in coordination, 
where applicable, with relevant states, Load Serving Entities, and 
New Large Loads—may issue more specific directives to specific 
retail customers. PJM will only direct load reduction of an aggregate 
MW IRAS within the zone or area. 
 
PJM’s filing is largely silent as to exactly how it will determine the MW amount 
when issuing an IRAS Action. PJM states that the “IRAS reduction MW quantity . . . will 
be based on the IRAS quantity PJM determined for the Delivery Year.”11 PJM’s filing 
describes how it determines the yearly IRAS quantity based on Eligible New Large Load 
Amounts,12 which will be less than or equal to the Electric Distributor’s Eligible New 
Large Load Amount for that year.13 But PJM’s Filing does not explain how PJM will 
determine the IRAS quantity it directs an Electric Distributor to cause to be reduced in a 
given emergency event in real-time.  
II. 
PJM Should Clarify How IRAS MW Quantity is Determined in Real-
Time to Protect Existing Customers from Unnecessary Shut-Off. 
Buckeye generally supports PJM’s proposal to ensure continued reliability for 
existing customers by issuing IRAS Actions during times of grid stress, which should 
 
loads’ differently for purposes of their retail tariffs, particularly those governing load reduction protocols. 
Thus, while PJM will determine the quantity of MW that load in a zone/area will need to be reduced by to 
maintain system reliability in the PJM Region, states may determine—under their own laws, policies, and 
definition of what constitutes ‘large load’—which resources will be called on to reduce load.”). 
11 Transmittal Letter at 83.  
12 Redlined Tariff, Attach. DD-4 § V(b) (“A New Large Load’s Eligible New Large Load Amount shall be 
determined as follows: (New Large Load’s registered peak load (in MW), as provided in the Large Load 
Registry) minus (the sum of all BYONC arrangements with the New Large Load in accordance with Tariff, 
Attachment DD-4, section VII divided by the Forecast Pool Requirement for the first Delivery Year in 
which the BYONC cleared an RPM Auction, plus Allocated RBP UCAP MW assigned to the New Large 
Load, in accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IX divided by the Forecast Pool Requirement 
for the first Delivery Year in which the Allocated RBP UCAP MW cleared an RPM Auction).”). 
13 Transmittal Letter at 70-72. As PJM describes, the maximum IRAS quantity will occur when the capacity 
shortfall exceeds the cumulative sum of all Eligible New Large Load Amounts, in which case all Eligible 
New Large Load Amounts need to be available to provide IRAS. If the capacity shortfall is less than that 
cumulative sum, then only Eligible New Large Loads Amounts equal to that shortfall must be available for 
IRAS. If there is no capacity shortfall, then no amount needs to be available for IRAS.

- 5 - 
 
facilitate New Large Loads not supported by new capacity (i.e., those contributing to 
reliability concerns) reducing load before existing customers are subject to curtailment. 
Additional clarification is needed, however, as to how IRAS Actions will be implemented 
in real-time to ensure that the mechanism does not unintentionally require that existing 
customers, including residential loads, be unnecessarily curtailed.  
As detailed below, PJM should clarify how the MW quantity that PJM directs 
Electric Distributors to drop in an IRAS Action will be determined in a manner that 
ensures that Electric Distributors are not required to reduce more load in real-time than is 
being operated by New Large Loads at that time. Buckeye is concerned that directing the 
Electric Distributor to reduce a specific amount of MW quantity based on registered peak 
load of New Large Loads determined for the Delivery Year will not match the actual 
amount of load being used by the New Large Loads in real-time. If PJM were allowed to 
direct IRAS quantities in real-time that exceed the real-time demand of New Large 
Loads, this mismatch between the peak load reported by the New Large Load in the 
registry and the amount of load the Large Load is using in real-time could require the 
Electric Distributor to reduce existing customers, including residential loads, to make up 
the difference. 
For example, assume the Large Load Registry for an Electric Distributor 
zone/area shows 3,000 MW of peak load attributable to three New Large Loads for the 
applicable delivery year with 1,000 MW of BYONC. That would result in 2,000 MW of 
Eligible New Large Load Amounts subject to IRAS. PJM issues a real-time IRAS Action 
that requires the Electric Distributor to reduce 2,000 MW of load based on the Electric 
Distributor’s maximum Eligible New Large Load Amount for that Delivery Year.

- 6 - 
 
However, in real-time, the demand of the three New Large Loads is only 1,500 MW 
(perhaps because one reduced usage in response to earlier alerts, or because one or more 
of the New Large Loads are not yet fully operational). 
Importantly, because the real-time load of the New Large Loads is just 
1,500 MW, the Electric Distributor would have no ability to meet a 2,000 MW reduction 
obligation from just the New Large Loads—even though those New Large Loads are the 
sole reason the IRAS obligation exists. As a result, in this scenario, the Electric 
Distributor would be forced to reduce 500 MW of load for existing customers, which 
may impact residential loads and other non-New Large Load end-users. Moreover, that 
additional 500 MW of curtailment from non-large load customers would be unnecessary, 
as an IRAS quantity equal to the New Large Load’s real-time load should be sufficient to 
address the reliability impacts of New Large Loads unsupported by new capacity. 
This outcome is clearly contrary to PJM’s intent, which is to base the IRAS load 
reduction obligation specifically on the extent to which New Large Loads have failed to 
cover their capacity obligations with new generation. Nothing in PJM’s desire to provide 
flexibility to states and Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authorities (“RERRAs”) 
suggests an intent that Electric Distributors would be forced to reduce existing customers’ 
load as a result of New Large Loads. Indeed, PJM’s emphasis that load curtailment is the 
last resort, with IRAS Actions coming well before that, confirms that existing customers 
are not intended to be forced to bear the burden of IRAS reductions. 
Buckeye asks that PJM clarify how the MW amounts Electric Distributors will be 
asked to curtail will be determined in a real-time IRAS Action, and whether this 
determination will consider the actual demand of the New Large Loads in real-time to

- 7 - 
 
avoid requiring impacts to existing customer load described above. Specifically, PJM 
should ensure that the amount of MWs the Electric Distributor is required to drop in 
response to an IRAS Action will not exceed the amount of MWs being used by the New 
Large Loads in real-time.14 This clarification will still allow the Electric Distributors, 
working with its applicable state or RERRA, to determine how the MW drop will be 
assigned to individual loads, while at the same time ensuring that Electric Distributors are 
not put in the position of being forced to drop existing load (the action of last resort to 
maintain grid integrity) to comply with an IRAS Action. 
To the extent that the proposed Tariff language must be revised to make this 
clarification, PJM should do so. To the extent PJM does not voluntarily do so, the 
Commission should direct it to make these changes in order to protect existing customers 
from reliability impacts caused by New Large Loads and to ensure just, reasonable, and 
not unduly discriminatory rates. At minimum, if PJM does not clarify this issue 
consistent with Buckeye’s limited comments herein, the Commission should issue a 
deficiency letter directing PJM to explain how the existing proposal is just, reasonable, 
and not unduly discriminatory.  
PJM has already consented to make modifications “consistent with PJM’s 
overarching objectives in this filing,”15 which the clarification described above would be. 
And although clarification of this issue is important to protecting everyday ratepayers, it 
is permissible because it would not result in an entirely different rate design than what 
 
14 For example, PJM should consider clarifying that the Electric Distributor would fulfill the IRAS Action 
by dropping the New Large Load to zero if the total IRAS Action MW directive exceeds the actual amount 
of New Large Load online in real-time. Where the New Large Load is an incremental increase of an 
existing load, the Electric Distributor would fulfill the IRAS Action by reducing the load to its prior output. 
15 Transmittal Letter at 122.

- 8 - 
 
PJM has proposed.16 Rather, it is a change to one element in order to ensure PJM’s IRAS 
proposal functions as intended and without forcing non-large load ratepayers to bear the 
reliability burdens caused by New Large Loads.17 
CONCLUSION 
 
For the reasons stated above, the Commission should (to the extent PJM does 
not do so on its own) require PJM to clarify how it will calculate the IRAS Action 
reduction quantity in real-time, including whether that amount could exceed New Large 
Load in real-time such that an Electric Distributor is forced to curtail other, existing 
customers. To the extent Tariff revisions are required to prevent this problem, the 
Commission should direct PJM to make those further revisions to the extent it does not 
do so voluntarily.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
16 Old Dominion Elec. Coop., 162 FERC ¶ 61,262, P 35 (2018) (“[T]he Commission may propose revisions 
to a section 205 filing that do not amount to an entirely different rate design or rate scheme, provided that 
the filing utility consents to the changes.” (citing NRG Power Mktg., LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108, 116-117 
(D.C. Cir. 2017))). 
17 See, e.g., Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,210, P 62 (2026) (directing a 
compliance filing “to incorporate into the Tariff language clarifying MISO’s stated intent” regarding one 
element of a filing to reform its tariff provisions on demand-side resources and certain supply-side 
resources participating during emergencies).
